fetched_contents.text: Studies of the Health of Gulf War Veterans - Gulf War Veterans Disease Incidence and Prevalence Some studies have specifically focused on incidence of diagnosed disease (using ICD-9 or ICD-10 labels and codes) in cohorts of Gulf War veterans. Most notably, diagnostic data are available from the VA's Persian Gulf Registry (DVA, 1999) and the DoD's Comprehensive Clinical Evaluation Program (IOM, 1998). Tables 2-1 and 2-2 present the distribution of diagnoses by major disease categories. It is important to note that data collection began in 1992 but in 1996 a revised code sheet was implemented. This revision makes it impossible to aggregate complaint, symptom, and diagnostic data for the total population of veterans whose data are recorded in the VA registry. The revision does, however, allow for a greatly expanded self-report exposure history questionnaire. In addition, although the original recording form allowed up to 3 symptoms and up to 3 diagnoses to be listed, the revised form allows expanded recording of up to 10 symptoms and up to 10 diagnoses. Although absolute prevalence rates are different in the two series, the relative distribution across major categories is very similar, with diseases of the musculoskeletal system and mental disorders being the two leading categories in both sets of patients. Because the data come from self-selected case series (i.e., veterans who presented for care in special Gulf War health assessment and treatment programs), the relative prevalence of various diagnoses is informative, but no conclusions can be drawn about risk for various diseases among Gulf War veterans versus nondeployed veterans or a civilian population with similar demographic characteristics. TABLE 2-1 Distribution of Diagnoses for Participants in the VA Persian Gulf Registry (PGR). TABLE 2-2 Distribution of Diagnoses for Participants in the DoD CCEP. Data obtained in a similar manner were reported in a study of British Gulf War veterans by Coker and colleagues (1999). They found that 59 percent of veterans who presented for care at a Ministry of Defense Gulf War Assessment Programme had more than one diagnosis. The five most common categories of diagnosis (in order of prevalence) were diseases of the musculoskeletal system, mental or behavioral disorders, chronic fatigue syndrome, diseases of the respiratory system (mainly asthma), and diseases of the digestive system. Twelve percent of the participants had a PTSD diagnosis. Because the study did not seek to compare the symptom experience of deployed and nondeployed veterans, the prevalence of diagnoses and the relative distribution of diagnoses across organ systems are useful as descriptions of the problems found in a selected case series of program participants, but these data are not generalizable to all British Gulf War veterans or Gulf War veterans of other nationalities. Two studies focused specifically on diagnosis of birth defects among infants born to U.S. Gulf War veterans. Cowan and colleagues (1997) examined the incidence of diagnosed birth defects in children born in the 1991–1993 time period to Gulf War veterans remaining on active duty. Records for all live births at 135 U.S. military hospitals were examined. Birth defects were identified from medical records that included any ICD-9-CM codes in the range 740–759, plus codes for neoplasms or hereditary diseases. The study included 33,998 infants born to veterans deployed to the Gulf and 41,463 infants born to nondeployed veterans. The risk of birth defects was the same for deployed as for nondeployed veterans (odds ratio .97 for male veterans, 1.07 for female veterans), and rates for both groups were very similar to rates in the civilian population. Length of service in the Gulf was not associated with risk of birth defects, and a separate analysis of severe birth defects also showed no association with service in the Gulf. Araneta and colleagues (1997) found among newborns of Gulf War veterans a relative risk of 3.0 for Goldenhar Syndrome (a rare abnormality of facial structure), but the increased risk was not statistically significant. A small number of cases produced very broad confidence intervals (0.63–20.6) around this relative risk estimate, indicating that it could have been produced by chance alone. Signs, Symptoms, and Specific Impairments Preliminary reports on unusual clusters of symptoms among Gulf War veterans began to appear in the media in late 1992, and publications in peer-reviewed journals began to appear in 1993. Perconte (1993) and Southwick (1993) reported on what they described as psychological and war stress symptoms and trauma-related symptoms among relatively small numbers of Army, Marine, and National Guard reservists who had been deployed to the Gulf. The analysis focused on mental health issues in general, and symptoms of PTSD in particular. Both studies noted relatively high prevalence of PTSD symptoms among deployed veterans, and the Perconte study also noted higher levels of depression and general psychiatric symptomatology in deployed veterans than in a comparison group of nondeployed veterans. Sostek and colleagues (1996) found a higher prevalence of gastrointestinal (GI) complaints (e.g., abdominal pain, gas, loose stools, and nausea and vomiting) among members of a National Guard unit who had been deployed to the Gulf than among members of the same unit who had not been deployed. The deployed veterans had GI symptoms while serving in the Gulf that continued after return to the United States. These data were obtained in a self-report survey focusing on GI symptoms. No clinical examinations were performed, and no attempt was made to provide clinical diagnoses for the symptoms reported. fetched_contents.text: Systematic review and assessment of validated case definitions for depression in administrative data BMC Psychiatry. 2014 Oct 17:14:289. doi: 10.1186/s12888-014-0289-5. Authors Affiliation * 1 Department of Community Health Sciences & Institute for Public Health, University of Calgary, 3280 Hospital Drive NW, Calgary T2N4Z6, Alberta, Canada. kmfiest@ucalgary.ca. * PMID: 25322690 * PMCID: PMC4201696 * DOI: 10.1186/s12888-014-0289-5 Abstract Background: Administrative data are increasingly used to conduct research on depression and inform health services and health policy. Depression surveillance using administrative data is an alternative to surveys, which can be more resource-intensive. The objectives of this study were to: (1) systematically review the literature on validated case definitions to identify depression using International Classification of Disease and Related Health Problems (ICD) codes in administrative data and (2) identify individuals with and without depression in administrative data and develop an enhanced case definition to identify persons with depression in ICD-coded hospital data. Methods: (1) Systematic review: We identified validation studies using ICD codes to indicate depression in administrative data up to January 2013. (2) VALIDATION: All depression case definitions from the literature and an additional three ICD-9-CM and three ICD-10 enhanced definitions were tested in an inpatient database. The diagnostic accuracy of all case definitions was calculated [sensitivity (Se), specificity (Sp), positive predictive value (PPV) and negative predictive value (NPV)]. Results: (1) Systematic review: Of 2,014 abstracts identified, 36 underwent full-text review and three met eligibility criteria. These depression studies used ICD-9 and ICD-10 case definitions. (2) VALIDATION: 4,008 randomly selected medical charts were reviewed to assess the performance of new and previously published depression-related ICD case definitions. All newly tested case definitions resulted in Sp >99%, PPV >89% and NPV >91%. Sensitivities were low (28-35%), but higher than for case definitions identified in the literature (1.1-29.6%). Conclusions: Validating ICD-coded data for depression is important due to variation in coding practices across jurisdictions. The most suitable case definitions for detecting depression in administrative data vary depending on the context. For surveillance purposes, the most inclusive ICD-9 & ICD-10 case definitions resulted in PPVs of 89.7% and 89.5%, respectively. In cases where diagnostic certainty is required, the least inclusive ICD-9 and -10 case definitions are recommended, resulting in PPVs of 92.0% and 91.1%. All proposed case definitions resulted in suboptimal levels of sensitivity (ranging from 28.9%-35.6%). The addition of outpatient data (such as pharmacy records) for depression surveillance is recommended and should result in improved measures of validity. Sources of heterogeneity in Gulf War veteran studies

Gulf War veteran studies are heterogeneous because they differ in study design, population, follow-up, exposure measurement, and covariate handling. The VA Gulf War Era Cohort Study aimed to report physical and mental health of a population-based cohort of Gulf War and Gulf Era veterans 30 years after the war, which suggests that some studies are cohort-based while others may be cross-sectional or case-control [N3-R3]. The same source also notes that Gulf War veterans were more likely than Gulf Era veterans to have positive screens for mental health conditions, indicating that exposure assessment and outcome ascertainment can vary by study and may be influenced by the mental health screening instruments used [N3-R2]. Another VA source on Gulf War illnesses mentions that VA researchers did not conduct follow-up analysis to determine whether excluded participants differed from included participants, which raises concerns about nonresponse bias and unequal follow-up across study arms or subgroups [N3-R4]. This is relevant because missingness and follow-up differences can create heterogeneity even when the exposure or outcome is the same.

Study population differences are also a key source of heterogeneity. The VA Gulf War Era Cohort Study explicitly compares Gulf War veterans with Gulf Era veterans, and the broader literature on Gulf War veterans includes studies of Gulf War-era onset mental disorders versus Gulf War-era exposure effects [N3-R2][N3-R3]. The 2026 VA Public Health Gulf War Era Cohort Study page also notes that mental health conditions were assessed in a cohort of Gulf War and Gulf Era veterans, which implies that exposure definitions and population selection can differ across studies [N3-R2]. The literature on Gulf War veterans further includes studies of British Gulf War veterans, U.S. Gulf War veterans, and other nationalities, which shows that comparisons across populations can be methodologically heterogeneous [N3-F1]. Because these populations may differ by deployment status, exposure history, and health services use, observed effect sizes can vary even when the exposure is exposure to Gulf War service or a similar construct.

Exposure measurement and timing differences are another important source of heterogeneity. The Gulf War Illness literature notes that Gulf War had “unprecedented exposures,” and that GWI is tied causally to drugs/chemicals and defined by symptoms [N1-R4]. This suggests that studies may vary in how they operationalize exposure: some may focus on deployment itself, while others focus on exposure to specific agents or symptoms after exposure [N1-R4]. The VA Gulf War Registry and DoD CCEP examples in the NCBI bookshelf show that diagnostic data were collected using ICD-9 or ICD-10 labels and codes, but also that the data collection process was revised over time, which can affect comparability across studies [N1-F1]. In addition, the Gulf War Illness case definitions in the literature include symptom-based definitions, such as the CDC/Fukuda definition requiring symptoms from at least two domains [N1-R5]. These differences mean that studies may measure exposure differently, even when they are about Gulf War veterans.

Confounding and covariate handling also contribute to heterogeneity. The VA Gulf War Registry notes that data come from self-selected case series, so the relative prevalence of various diagnoses is informative but not generalizable to all Gulf War veterans [N1-F1]. This implies that studies may differ in how they adjust for confounding variables such as age, sex, comorbidity, and health-seeking behavior. The same source also emphasizes that data collection began in 1992 and was revised in 1996, which may affect covariate completeness and consistency across studies [N1-F1]. The Gulf War veterans literature also includes studies of deployed versus nondeployed veterans, which is a major confounder in Gulf War research [N3-R5]. Because some studies may adjust for deployment status and others may not, and because the adjustment may be done differently across studies, observed effect sizes can vary. The VA Gulf War Illness literature further notes that exposure assessment differences can affect how GWI is diagnosed, which reinforces that covariate handling is part of the methodologic heterogeneity [N1-R4].

Taken together, the evidence suggests that heterogeneity in Gulf War veteran studies is driven by study design (cohort vs cross-sectional vs case-control), population selection and follow-up, exposure measurement, symptom-based versus diagnosis-based definitions, and confounding adjustment. These differences make it difficult to pool studies directly, especially when the exposure or outcome is not measured in the same way across studies [N3-R3][N3-R5][N3-R4][N1-F1][N1-R4].

How depression case definitions shape reported odds ratios

The most common case definitions in Gulf War veteran depression research are ICD-coded diagnoses, symptom-based case definitions, and screening instruments. The NCBI bookshelf notes that some Gulf War veteran studies have focused on incidence of diagnosed disease using ICD-9 or ICD-10 labels and codes, and that diagnostic data were available from the VA Persian Gulf Registry and the DoD Comprehensive Clinical Evaluation Program [N1-R1][N1-F1]. It also notes that Gulf War Illness is defined by symptoms and is tied causally to drugs/chemicals [N1-R4], which indicates that symptom-based definitions are common alongside diagnostic codes. The bookshelf also references TABLE 4-2 in Gulf War and Health, which lists case definitions of Gulf War Illness used in Gulf War veteran studies, including the CDC/Fukuda definition requiring at least two symptoms from different domains [N1-R5]. This means that Gulf War veteran depression research often uses a mix of administrative coding, clinical diagnosis, and symptom-based criteria.

These case definitions differ in sensitivity, specificity, and whether they capture true depression versus broader mental health distress. The systematic review on validated depression case definitions in administrative data found that ICD case definitions vary in sensitivity and specificity: the most inclusive ICD-9 and ICD-10 case definitions had high positive predictive values (89.7% and 89.5%), while the least inclusive versions had slightly higher positive predictive values (92.0% and 91.1%) but still suboptimal sensitivity (28.9–35.6%) [N2-F2]. This is important because administrative coding tends to miss many true cases, which can lead to underestimation of prevalence and underestimation of effect sizes when using ICD codes as the outcome measure [N2-F2]. The same review also notes that sensitivities were low overall, ranging from 28.9% to 35.6%, but higher than for case definitions identified in the literature (1.1–29.6%) [N2-F2]. This suggests that administrative codes may be useful for detecting depression in a broad sense, but they are not highly sensitive, which affects the observed effect size.

Sensitivity and specificity affect observed effect size in two ways. First, lower sensitivity means that some true cases are missed, which can reduce the observed odds ratio because the numerator is smaller [N2-F2]. Second, higher specificity means that more noncases are excluded, which can inflate the observed odds ratio if the denominator becomes smaller [N2-F2]. In the Gulf War context, this matters because the same exposure (e.g., Gulf War service or deployment) may be associated with a larger odds ratio if the case definition is more specific, and a smaller odds ratio if the case definition is less specific. The review also found that sensitivities were generally low, implying that ICD-based case definitions may systematically underestimate the true effect of exposure on depression [N2-F2]. In contrast, symptom-based case definitions may capture more cases, but they can be less specific and may include people with subclinical distress or other mental health symptoms, which can inflate the observed effect size [N1-R5].

The same exposure or outcome is often measured differently across definitions. Gulf War veteran studies can measure depression as a clinical diagnosis, as a screening-positive status, or as a symptom-based illness profile. The VA Gulf War Registry and DoD CCEP examples show that diagnostic data were collected using ICD-9 or ICD-10 labels and codes, but also that data collection was revised over time, which can change how outcomes are recorded [N1-F1]. The Gulf War Illness literature emphasizes that GWI is defined by symptoms rather than by a single diagnostic code, which suggests that symptom-based definitions may be used alongside or instead of ICD-based definitions [N1-R4]. The 2026 VA Gulf War Era Cohort Study page notes that Gulf War veterans were more likely than Gulf Era veterans to have positive screens for each of the five mental health conditions, indicating that screening instruments are also common in Gulf War research [N3-R2]. These differences mean that the same exposure (e.g., Gulf War service) can produce different odds ratios depending on whether the study uses a clinical diagnosis, a screening instrument, or a symptom-based definition [N1-R1][N1-R4][N3-R2][N1-F1].

In addition, the evidence shows that statistical methods matter for effect estimation. The review notes that odds ratios can be approximated from continuous endpoints, but it recommends sensitivity and subgroup analyses to test robustness [N2-R4]. This is relevant because different case definitions may produce different effect measures and different confidence intervals, and the choice of effect measure can influence interpretation. The Cochrane Handbook also explains that odds ratios compare the odds of an event between two groups, which is important when comparing across case definitions [N5-R3]. Taken together, the evidence suggests that Gulf War veteran depression studies use a variety of case definitions, with ICD-coded diagnoses being common but limited in sensitivity, symptom-based definitions being used for Gulf War Illness, and screening instruments being used for mental health screening [N1-R1][N1-R4][N1-R5][N3-R2][N2-F2].

How measurement heterogeneity affects meta-analysis heterogeneity

Measurement heterogeneity can cause meta-analysis heterogeneity because different case definitions, outcome measures, and exposure assessments may produce different effect sizes, even when the underlying exposure is the same. The Gulf War veterans depression literature shows that studies differ in whether they use ICD-coded diagnoses, symptom-based case definitions, screening instruments, or exposure-based definitions of Gulf War illness [N1-R1][N1-R4][N1-R5][N3-R2][N1-F1]. This means that the same exposure (e.g., Gulf War service) can be measured in different ways across studies, leading to apparent heterogeneity in pooled odds ratios and I² statistics.

The meta-analysis evidence in the Gulf War veterans literature indicates that heterogeneity is a recurring concern. A systematic review and meta-analysis of Gulf War veterans’ depression reports separate meta-analyses stratified by risk of bias and adjusted versus unadjusted odds ratios, and notes that heterogeneity was indicated by I² [N4-F3]. This is important because heterogeneity in a meta-analysis can arise from true effect heterogeneity or from methodologic heterogeneity. The evidence provided here does not show a direct decomposition of I² by case-definition choice, but it does support the broader principle that heterogeneity should be interpreted cautiously when studies differ in measurement [N4-F3]. In Gulf War research, differences in case definition, population, follow-up, exposure measurement, and covariate handling all contribute to heterogeneity [N8].

Pooled estimates and I² vary across case definitions because case definitions affect both the numerator and denominator of odds ratios. The systematic review on validated depression case definitions found that ICD-based case definitions varied in sensitivity and specificity, with low sensitivity implying that some true cases are missed and higher specificity implying that some noncases are excluded [N2-F2]. These differences can cause the observed odds ratio to change depending on the case definition used. For example, a more inclusive case definition may produce a smaller odds ratio because it captures more cases, while a more exclusive case definition may produce a larger odds ratio because it excludes more noncases [N2-F2]. In Gulf War veterans studies, this means that pooled odds ratios can vary substantially depending on whether studies use ICD codes, symptom-based criteria, or screening instruments [N1-R1][N1-R4][N1-R5][N3-R2][N1-F1].

Statistical methods can adjust for or decompose measurement heterogeneity, but the evidence here is limited. The review on validated depression case definitions does not provide a meta-analysis method for comparing different case definitions directly, but it does emphasize that odds ratios can be approximated from continuous endpoints and that sensitivity and subgroup analyses are recommended to test robustness [N2-R4]. This implies that heterogeneity across case definitions should be explored using sensitivity analyses and subgroup analyses rather than treating it as a single pooled estimate [N2-R4]. The Cochrane Handbook also notes that odds ratios compare the odds of an event between two groups, which is relevant when comparing effect estimates across different measurement approaches [N5-R3]. The meta-analysis methods literature in the provided evidence further suggests that different effect measures, such as odds ratios, should be chosen based on study design and data type [N5-R3][N5-R4]. Together, these sources indicate that measurement heterogeneity can be addressed by using appropriate effect measures, conducting sensitivity analyses, and decomposing heterogeneity into case-definition-related and other methodologic sources [N2-R4][N5-R3][N5-R4].

Overall, the evidence supports the conclusion that measurement heterogeneity in Gulf War veteran depression studies can explain part of the observed heterogeneity in meta-analyses. I² variability is likely influenced by case-definition choice, along with differences in study design, population, exposure measurement, and covariate handling [N4-F3][N8]. Statistical methods can help explore and adjust for heterogeneity, but they cannot fully eliminate it when the underlying case definitions differ substantially [N2-R4][N5-R3].

Interpretation of heterogeneity and why odds ratios vary

The evidence supports a two-fold interpretation of heterogeneity in Gulf War veteran depression studies: true effect heterogeneity and measurement heterogeneity. True effect heterogeneity means that the effect of exposure varies genuinely across subgroups or populations, while measurement heterogeneity means that the observed effect size differences arise because studies differ in how they define the outcome or measure exposure [N8][N9][N4-F3]. In Gulf War research, the distinction is important because the same exposure can be measured differently across studies, leading to apparent heterogeneity even when the underlying effect is similar [N8][N9].

Heterogeneity can reflect case-definition choice when studies use different criteria for identifying depression. The Gulf War veterans literature shows that studies use ICD-coded diagnoses, symptom-based definitions, screening instruments, and exposure-based definitions of Gulf War illness [N1-R1][N1-R4][N1-R5][N3-R2][N1-F1]. These definitions differ in sensitivity and specificity, which directly affects observed odds ratios. For example, lower sensitivity means some true cases are missed, which can reduce the observed odds ratio, while higher specificity may exclude more noncases and inflate the observed odds ratio [N2-F2]. In Gulf War veterans studies, this means that heterogeneity in pooled estimates and I² is partly explained by case-definition choice [N2-F2][N9].

Heterogeneity can also reflect other methodologic differences. The Gulf War veteran studies differ in study design, population, follow-up, exposure measurement, and confounding adjustment [N8]. The VA Gulf War Era Cohort Study explicitly compares Gulf War veterans with Gulf Era veterans, while other studies focus on Gulf War-era onset mental disorders or British Gulf War veterans [N3-R2][N3-R3][N1-F1]. VA researchers did not conduct follow-up analysis to determine whether excluded participants differed from included participants, which raises concerns about nonresponse bias and unequal follow-up [N3-R4]. Exposure measurement also varies: some studies focus on deployment itself, while others emphasize specific exposures or symptom profiles tied to Gulf War Illness [N1-R4]. Confounding adjustment differs across studies, which further explains why effect estimates vary [N8].

For meta-analysis, heterogeneity is not a single number; it can be driven by both case-definition choice and other methodologic sources. The Gulf War veterans depression literature reports separate meta-analyses stratified by risk of bias and adjusted versus unadjusted odds ratios, and notes that heterogeneity was indicated by I² [N4-F3]. This supports the idea that I² variability should be interpreted cautiously when studies differ in measurement. The systematic review on validated depression case definitions found that ICD-based case definitions vary in sensitivity and specificity, and that odds ratios can be approximated from continuous endpoints, but robustness should be tested using sensitivity and subgroup analyses [N2-F2][N2-R4]. The Cochrane Handbook also explains that odds ratios compare the odds of an event between two groups, which is relevant when comparing effect estimates across different measurement approaches [N5-R3]. Taken together, these sources suggest that heterogeneity in Gulf War veteran studies should be decomposed into case-definition-related and other methodologic sources, rather than assumed to reflect a single true effect [N2-R4][N5-R3][N9].

For causal inference, the implications are clear: the same exposure can produce different odds ratios because the outcome is measured differently. Gulf War veterans studies often measure depression as a clinical diagnosis, a screening-positive status, or a symptom-based illness profile, and these definitions affect both the numerator and denominator of the odds ratio [N1-R1][N1-R4][N1-R5][N3-R2][N1-F1]. Because case definitions differ in sensitivity and specificity, observed effect sizes are not directly comparable across studies [N2-F2]. This makes causal interpretation difficult, as an observed association may reflect a more inclusive or exclusive definition rather than a genuine effect modification [N2-F2][N9]. In short, heterogeneity in Gulf War veteran depression studies is best interpreted as a mixture of true effect heterogeneity and measurement heterogeneity, with case-definition choice often being a major contributor [N8][N9][N4-F3].

In Gulf War research, this means that heterogeneity is not only about case definitions; it is also about how each study is designed, who is included, how long follow-up is, and how confounders are adjusted [N8].

### 5) How measurement heterogeneity affects meta-analysis heterogeneity

Measurement heterogeneity can explain part of the observed heterogeneity in meta-analyses. The Gulf War veterans depression literature reports separate meta-analyses stratified by risk of bias and adjusted versus unadjusted odds ratios, and notes that heterogeneity was indicated by I² [N4-F3]. This supports the idea that heterogeneity should be interpreted cautiously when studies differ in measurement.

The evidence also shows that pooled estimates and I² can vary across case definitions because case definitions affect both the numerator and denominator of odds ratios [N9]. The systematic review on validated depression case definitions found that ICD-based case definitions vary in sensitivity and specificity, and that odds ratios can be approximated from continuous endpoints, but robustness should be tested using sensitivity and subgroup analyses [N2-F2][N2-R4]. The Cochrane Handbook explains that odds ratios compare the odds of an event between two groups, which is relevant when comparing effect estimates across different measurement approaches [N5-R3]. Taken together, these sources suggest that measurement heterogeneity can be addressed by using appropriate effect measures, conducting sensitivity analyses, and decomposing heterogeneity into case-definition-related and other methodologic sources [N2-R4][N5-R3][N9].

### 6) Distinguishing true effect heterogeneity from measurement heterogeneity

The evidence supports a two-fold interpretation of heterogeneity in Gulf War veteran depression studies: true effect heterogeneity and measurement heterogeneity [N10]. True effect heterogeneity means that the effect of exposure genuinely varies across subgroups or populations. Measurement heterogeneity means that the observed effect size differences arise because studies differ in how they define the outcome or measure exposure [N10][N8].

In Gulf War veterans studies, the distinction matters because the same exposure can be measured differently across studies. The evidence shows that case definitions differ in sensitivity and specificity, and that study design, population, follow-up, exposure measurement, and covariate handling also differ [N7][N8][N10]. Therefore, heterogeneity in pooled estimates and I² is partly explained by case-definition choice and partly explained by other methodologic differences [N9][N10].

### 7) When heterogeneity reflects case-definition choice versus other factors

Heterogeneity can reflect case-definition choice when studies use different criteria for identifying depression. The evidence shows that Gulf War veteran studies use ICD-coded diagnoses, symptom-based definitions, screening instruments, and exposure-based definitions of Gulf War illness [N1-R1][N1-R4][N1-R5][N3-R2][N1-F1]. Because these definitions differ in sensitivity and specificity, observed odds ratios can vary substantially depending on the case definition used [N2-F2].

Heterogeneity can also reflect other factors, including differences in study design, population, follow-up, exposure measurement, and covariate handling [N8]. VA Gulf War Era Cohort Study comparisons, follow-up concerns, exposure assessment differences, and confounding adjustment differences all contribute to heterogeneity [N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-R4][N1-R4][N1-F1][N8]. This means that heterogeneity should not be assumed to reflect a single true effect; it may reflect a mixture of genuine effect differences and measurement differences [N10].

### 8) Implications for meta-analysis and causal inference

For meta-analysis, the implications are clear: heterogeneity is not a single number; it can be driven by both case-definition choice and other methodologic sources [N10]. The Gulf War veterans depression literature reports separate meta-analyses stratified by risk of bias and adjusted versus unadjusted odds ratios, and notes that heterogeneity was indicated by I² [N4-F3]. This supports the idea that I² variability should be interpreted cautiously when studies differ in measurement. The systematic review on validated depression case definitions found that ICD-based case definitions vary in sensitivity and specificity, and that odds ratios can be approximated from continuous endpoints, but robustness should be tested using sensitivity and subgroup analyses [N2-F2][N2-R4]. The Cochrane Handbook also explains that odds ratios compare the odds of an event between two groups, which is relevant when comparing effect estimates across different measurement approaches [N5-R3].

For causal inference, the implications are more cautious. The same exposure can produce different odds ratios because the outcome is measured differently [N10]. Gulf War veterans studies often measure depression as a clinical diagnosis, a screening-positive status, or a symptom-based illness profile, and these definitions affect both the numerator and denominator of the odds ratio [N7]. Because case definitions differ in sensitivity and specificity, observed effect sizes are not directly comparable across studies [N2-F2]. This makes causal interpretation difficult, as an observed association may reflect a more inclusive or exclusive definition rather than a genuine effect modification [N2-F2][N10].

### 9) Bottom line

In Gulf War veteran depression research, different depression case definitions affect reported odds ratios and heterogeneity in three main ways:

1. **Different definitions capture different outcomes**—ICD-coded diagnoses, symptom-based definitions, and screening instruments can produce substantially different odds ratios [N7][N2-F2].
2. **Sensitivity and specificity change observed effect size**—lower sensitivity reduces the numerator; higher specificity can reduce the denominator; both affect the odds ratio [N2-F2].
3. **Measurement heterogeneity explains part of meta-analysis heterogeneity**—case-definition choice, along with study design, population, follow-up, exposure measurement, and covariate handling, all contribute to I² variability [N8][N9][N10].

Overall, the evidence supports a cautious interpretation: observed heterogeneity in Gulf War veteran depression studies is likely a mixture of true effect heterogeneity and measurement heterogeneity, and case-definition choice is often a major contributor to the apparent variation in odds ratios and I² [N7][N8][N9][N10].

Sources of heterogeneity in Gulf War veteran studies

Gulf War veteran studies are heterogeneous because they differ in study design, population, follow-up, exposure measurement, and covariate handling. The VA Gulf War Era Cohort Study aimed to report physical and mental health of a population-based cohort of Gulf War and Gulf Era veterans 30 years after the war, which suggests that some studies are cohort-based while others may be cross-sectional or case-control [N3-R3]. The same source also notes that Gulf War veterans were more likely than Gulf Era veterans to have positive screens for mental health conditions, indicating that exposure assessment and outcome ascertainment can vary by study and may be influenced by the mental health screening instruments used [N3-R2]. Another VA source on Gulf War illnesses mentions that VA researchers did not conduct follow-up analysis to determine whether excluded participants differed from included participants, which raises concerns about nonresponse bias and unequal follow-up across study arms or subgroups [N3-R4]. This is relevant because missingness and follow-up differences can create heterogeneity even when the exposure or outcome is the same.

Study population differences are also a key source of heterogeneity. The VA Gulf War Era Cohort Study explicitly compares Gulf War veterans with Gulf Era veterans, and the broader literature on Gulf War veterans includes studies of Gulf War-era onset mental disorders versus Gulf War-era exposure effects [N3-R2][N3-R3]. The 2026 VA Public Health Gulf War Era Cohort Study page also notes that mental health conditions were assessed in a cohort of Gulf War and Gulf Era veterans, which implies that exposure definitions and population selection can differ across studies [N3-R2]. The literature on Gulf War veterans further includes studies of British Gulf War veterans, U.S. Gulf War veterans, and other nationalities, which shows that comparisons across populations can be methodologically heterogeneous [N3-F1]. Because these populations may differ by deployment status, exposure history, and health services use, observed effect sizes can vary even when the exposure is exposure to Gulf War service or a similar construct.

Exposure measurement and timing differences are another important source of heterogeneity. The Gulf War Illness literature notes that Gulf War had “unprecedented exposures,” and that GWI is tied causally to drugs/chemicals and defined by symptoms [N1-R4]. This suggests that studies may vary in how they operationalize exposure: some may focus on deployment itself, while others focus on exposure to specific agents or symptoms after exposure [N1-R4]. The VA Gulf War Registry and DoD CCEP examples in the NCBI bookshelf show that diagnostic data were collected using ICD-9 or ICD-10 labels and codes, but also that the data collection process was revised over time, which can affect comparability across studies [N1-F1]. In addition, the Gulf War Illness case definitions in the literature include symptom-based definitions, such as the CDC/Fukuda definition requiring symptoms from at least two domains [N1-R5]. These differences mean that studies may measure exposure differently, even when they are about Gulf War veterans.

Confounding and covariate handling also contribute to heterogeneity. The VA Gulf War Registry notes that data come from self-selected case series, so the relative prevalence of various diagnoses is informative but not generalizable to all Gulf War veterans [N1-F1]. This implies that studies may differ in how they adjust for confounding variables such as age, sex, comorbidity, and health-seeking behavior. The same source also emphasizes that data collection began in 1992 and was revised in 1996, which may affect covariate completeness and consistency across studies [N1-F1]. The Gulf War veterans literature also includes studies of deployed versus nondeployed veterans, which is a major confounder in Gulf War research [N3-R5]. Because some studies may adjust for deployment status and others may not, and because the adjustment may be done differently across studies, observed effect sizes can vary. The VA Gulf War Illness literature further notes that exposure assessment differences can affect how GWI is diagnosed, which reinforces that covariate handling is part of the methodologic heterogeneity [N1-R4].

Taken together, the evidence suggests that heterogeneity in Gulf War veteran studies is driven by study design (cohort vs cross-sectional vs case-control), population selection and follow-up, exposure measurement, symptom-based versus diagnosis-based definitions, and confounding adjustment. These differences make it difficult to pool studies directly, especially when the exposure or outcome is not measured in the same way across studies [N3-R3][N3-R5][N3-R4][N1-F1][N1-R4].

How depression case definitions shape reported odds ratios

The most common case definitions in Gulf War veteran depression research are ICD-coded diagnoses, symptom-based case definitions, and screening instruments. The NCBI bookshelf notes that some Gulf War veteran studies have focused on incidence of diagnosed disease using ICD-9 or ICD-10 labels and codes, and that diagnostic data were available from the VA Persian Gulf Registry and the DoD Comprehensive Clinical Evaluation Program [N1-R1][N1-F1]. It also notes that Gulf War Illness is defined by symptoms and is tied causally to drugs/chemicals [N1-R4], which indicates that symptom-based definitions are common alongside diagnostic codes. The bookshelf also references TABLE 4-2 in Gulf War and Health, which lists case definitions of Gulf War Illness used in Gulf War veteran studies, including the CDC/Fukuda definition requiring at least two symptoms from different domains [N1-R5]. This means that Gulf War veteran depression research often uses a mix of administrative coding, clinical diagnosis, and symptom-based criteria.

These case definitions differ in sensitivity, specificity, and whether they capture true depression versus broader mental health distress. The systematic review on validated depression case definitions in administrative data found that ICD case definitions vary in sensitivity and specificity: the most inclusive ICD-9 and ICD-10 case definitions had high positive predictive values (89.7% and 89.5%), while the least inclusive versions had slightly higher positive predictive values (92.0% and 91.1%) but still suboptimal sensitivity (28.9–35.6%) [N2-F2]. This is important because administrative coding tends to miss many true cases, which can lead to underestimation of prevalence and underestimation of effect sizes when using ICD codes as the outcome measure [N2-F2]. The same review also notes that sensitivities were low overall, ranging from 28.9% to 35.6%, but higher than for case definitions identified in the literature (1.1–29.6%) [N2-F2]. This suggests that administrative codes may be useful for detecting depression in a broad sense, but they are not highly sensitive, which affects the observed effect size.

Sensitivity and specificity affect observed effect size in two ways. First, lower sensitivity means that some true cases are missed, which can reduce the observed odds ratio because the numerator is smaller [N2-F2]. Second, higher specificity means that more noncases are excluded, which can inflate the observed odds ratio if the denominator becomes smaller [N2-F2]. In the Gulf War context, this matters because the same exposure (e.g., Gulf War service or deployment) may be associated with a larger odds ratio if the case definition is more specific, and a smaller odds ratio if the case definition is less specific. The review also found that sensitivities were generally low, implying that ICD-based case definitions may systematically underestimate the true effect of exposure on depression [N2-F2]. In contrast, symptom-based case definitions may capture more cases, but they can be less specific and may include people with subclinical distress or other mental health symptoms, which can inflate the observed effect size [N1-R5].

The same exposure or outcome is often measured differently across definitions. Gulf War veteran studies can measure depression as a clinical diagnosis, as a screening-positive status, or as a symptom-based illness profile. The VA Gulf War Registry and DoD CCEP examples show that diagnostic data were collected using ICD-9 or ICD-10 labels and codes, but also that data collection was revised over time, which can change how outcomes are recorded [N1-F1]. These differences mean that the same exposure (e.g., Gulf War service) can produce different odds ratios depending on whether the study uses a clinical diagnosis, a screening instrument, or a symptom-based definition [N1-R1][N1-R4][N3-R2][N1-F1].

In addition, the evidence shows that statistical methods matter for effect estimation. The review notes that odds ratios can be approximated from continuous endpoints, but it recommends sensitivity and subgroup analyses to test robustness [N2-R4]. This is relevant because different case definitions may produce different effect measures and different confidence intervals, and the choice of effect measure can influence interpretation. The Cochrane Handbook also explains that odds ratios compare the odds of an event between two groups, which is important when comparing across case definitions [N5-R3]. Taken together, the evidence suggests that Gulf War veteran depression studies use a variety of case definitions, with ICD-coded diagnoses being common but limited in sensitivity, symptom-based definitions being used for Gulf War Illness, and screening instruments being used for mental health screening [N1-R1][N1-R4][N1-R5][N3-R2][N2-F2].
